newsitem.title: USA: CLIMATE TALKS EXPECTATIONS DROP - U.S. INDUSTRIES.
newsitem.headline: CLIMATE TALKS EXPECTATIONS DROP - U.S. INDUSTRIES.

text.p: Expectations that countries will sign a strong agreement to curb global climate change have dropped after negotiating sessions in Bonn this week, oil and coal industry representatives said Thursday.

"We felt expectations were being lowered, and in our view that would be a positive development because there is no need for a rush to judgement," Gail McDonald, president of the Global Climate Coalition, said in a telephone briefing from Bonn.
The GCC is funded by the fossil fuel industry, which would be hard-hit if countries adopt strict targets and timetables to reduce industrial pollution that is changing the world's climate.

McDonald and John Grasser, vice president for external communications with the National Mining Association, said they thought a "two-step process" might evolve in which countries would agree to a fairly vague document at the talks scheduled to conclude in December in Kyoto, Japan.

"You could come away from Kyoto claiming partial success, but it would be a kind of fill-in-the-blanks protocol. So maybe over the next two years you could continue negotiating what the targets and timetables are," Grasser said.

Grasser and McDonald also said other countries appeared to consider a U.S. Senate resolution calling for developing countries to be included in the climate change treaty as strictly a United States issue.
"There seemed to be a real concerted effort not to talk about it," McDonald said.
"The negotiators need to realize that requirements of the resolution need to be met before there is any hope the Senate will ratify a treaty," Grasser said.

The Senate on July 25 unanimously passed a resolution calling on the Clinton administration to reject a climate change treaty unless it puts binding commitments on developing countries to reduce their pollution in the same timeframe as industrialized countries.
